title: Tamil Nadu life convict Selvam’s book Oru Thooku Kaithiyin Vaakumoolam wins Iyal Award of Canada
author: B. Kolappan
content_html:
Oru Thooku Kaithiyin Vaakumoolam (Testimony of a Death Warrant Prisoner), penned by life convict C. Selvam, has been selected for the Iyal Award for non-fiction by the Canada-based Tamil Literary Garden. This is probably the first time that the award has gone to a writer who has been living in prison for 32 years.

“I consider it an award for my reading. I could not study beyond Class 9, and reading sustained me in prison all these years,” said Selvam, who is now lodged in Vellore prison, currently out on parole. Selvam, a native of Thenthamaraikulam in Kanniyakumari district, said his favourite authors include Sundara Ramasamy, S. Ramakrishnan, Nanjil Nadan and Jayamohan.

Selvam also received a message from noted Sri Lankan writer A. Muthulingam, who lives in Canada, congratulating him on the book award. The award carries 1000 Canada Dollars.

C. Selvam, author of Oru Thooku Kaithiyin Vaakumoolam (Testimony of a Death Warrant Prisoner) | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

Selvam and his associates surrendered before a court in Nagercoil in connection with a murder in 1994. Though he and his friends Radhakrishnan and Shiekmeeran were awarded the death sentence, it was later commuted to life imprisonment by the President, on the condition that they spend the rest of their lives in prison.

In prison, Selvam started reading books, and his voracious reading resulted in a memoir that was released in December 2025. It was made possible by Badri Seshadri of Kizhakku Pathippagam, who had a chance encounter with Selvam in Tiruchi jail, where he was lodged in connection with his alleged remarks against the judiciary. Justice K. Chandru wrote the foreword to the book.

The book, surpasses even gripping crime thrillers and films, strongly advocates prison reforms and truthfully records life behind bars. Justice Chandru said he had decided to write the foreword because Selvam had written the truth.

Mr. Seshadri said the book was likely to win many awards as it seemed to have touched people across multiple domains, not just for its literary aspects but also for the way it dealt with legal issues. “It has made a significant impact on the legal fraternity, including judges,” he said.

A press release from the Tamil Literary Garden said the Lifetime Achievement Award would go to Trotsky Marudhu, the fiction award to writer Thirusenthalai, the non-fiction award to C. Selvan and Sankar Saravanan, the poetry award to Karunakaran, and the translation award to Geetha Sukumaran.

The organisers of the award have asked Selvam to depute a representative to collect the award on his behalf.

title: Clash erupts between Andhra, North East region students in nursing college, one girl hurt in Kakinada
author: T. Appala Naidu
content_html:
One student from Andhra Pradesh was injured in a clash that erupted between students from the State and the North Eastern region in S.K. College of Nursing in Kakinada city on Saturday (August 22, 2026).

Tension prevailed in the nursing college hostel after the students from the North East region lodged a complaint with Sarpavaram police stating that one of the students’ cell phone was stolen by some one.

The two groups clashed after the Andhra Pradesh students learnt about the police complaint. One girl, who received injuries on her head in the clash, was treated in Government General Hospital in Kakinada.

The Manipur students have reportedly shared the prevailing environment on the college campus with their Chief Minister, Yumnam Khemchand, raising alarm on their safety on the college campus. On being alerted by the Manipur government and higher authorities of Andhra Pradesh, Kakinada District Collector M.N. Harendhira Prasad and SP G. Bindu Madhav deployed a team of officials to maintain peace on the campus on Saturday. 

In a joint statement, Mr. Harendhira Prasad has stated; “The clash erupted between the groups of Telugu students and those from Manipur and Nagaland over theft of a phone of a Manipur student. The campus returned to normalcy after talks with the two groups”.

Mr. Harendhira Prasad has added that as many as 31 students of Manipur and Nagaland have been provided accommodation separately on Saturday night itself to guarantee them safety on the campus. 

Mr. Bindu Madhav has stated that talks would be held on Sunday (August 23) with the students on the college campus to maintain peace and harmony. 

Later, in an audio statement, the North Eastern region students thanked the officials concerned for their intervention and addressing their concerns on Saturday. Mr. Harendhira Prasad has said that the college management has been directed to provide separate accommodation for the North East region students on campus.

title: News in Frames | Toxic water runs deep
author: Shashi Shekhar Kashyap
content_html:
Decades of improper industrial waste management have contaminated groundwater with toxic hexavalent chromium across parts of three districts of Uttar Pradesh, exposing villagers to unsafe water and serious health risks.

Groundwater from handpumps glows bright yellow in different villages of these districts — a telltale sign of toxic hexavalent chromium contamination. Patches of yellow-green earth can also be seen in villages across these districts, revealing the illegal dumps and toxicity hiding beneath the surface.

The dumping started from 1976, as per the National Green Tribunal (NGT). But it was scattered across different districts at different points of time.

The earliest and largest chromium dump came up around 1976 in Rania, Kanpur Dehat, as per NGT reports. There were 62,225 metric tonnes of chromium waste dumped there. It was removed only about a year ago, following NGT orders and missed deadlines. There is an NGT direction to erect a boundary wall around it to minimise the dust from flying out, but the hazards remain.

Over the last five years, the government collected blood samples of people living in the affected areas. It was found that 73%-96% of the samples had levels of hexavalent chromium above safe limits, according to a 2025 government report. But despite years of complaints and legal intervention, the government’s efforts to identify contaminated areas, provide safe drinking water and healthcare, and clean up toxic waste remain slow and inadequate.

Sadly, many villages with contaminated groundwater or chemical dumps are not even part of the State government’s list of identified chromium-affected areas, indicating that the actual affected area is even larger than what the government has accepted so far, and thousands more people could be at risk.

Text by Nikhil M. Babu
